name: Passage des Panoramas
short_description: Oldest covered passage in Paris (1799), first public space in the city to have gas lighting in 1817, lined with stamp dealers and restaurants

beats.script_body: Passage des Panoramas was the first place in Paris to be gaslit, in 1817 — a dazzling novelty that drew the fashionable set to promenade here. The passage took its name from two circular Panoramas installed at the site: vast painted canvases that transported spectators to bloody battlefields or peaceful foreign lands. The concept had been invented and patented by the Irish-born painter Robert Barker in 1787, and the Paris installations became the dernier cri. The passage also housed the elegant Café Véron and the pastry shop Félix, making it one of the highlights of early 19th-century Paris.
beats.source_passage: Passage des Panoramas was one of the highlights of Paris in the last century, the first place in the city to be gaslit, in 1817

opening_hours_basis: A covered arcade with grilles that close, so gated, but its exact opening hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Covered arcade you walk through end to end, lined with stamp dealers, old shopfronts and restaurants to browse, about 15 minutes; it is itself the space, nothing separate to enter.
judgement_basis: A narrow covered arcade with glass shopfronts at child height, only paid restaurant seating, echoing acoustics, and gates that close it at night.
queue_basis: A covered public passage open at both ends with no door, ticket, or screening; you walk through freely.

name: Theatre des Varietes
short_description: Historic theatre on Boulevard Montmartre where Offenbach's operettas premiered, opened 1807

beats.script_body: At no. 7 Boulevard Montmartre, the Théâtre des Variétés still stands — the stage where Hortense Schneider created a sensation with Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse de Gérolstein in 1867. The premiere coincided with the Universal Exposition, and the audience included Napoleon III, the Prince of Wales, the Emperor of Russia, and Bismarck. Schneider's box became known as 'the passage of princes.' Next door at no. 9, the Café des Variétés had been a stronghold of Parisian literati until 1870.
physical_cues: Théâtre des Variétés still stands at no. 7 Boulevard Montmartre
beats.source_passage: Le Théatre des Variétés, where Hortense Schneider created a sensation with Offenbach's La Grande Duchesse in 1867, still stands

opening_hours_basis: A working theatre entered by ticket, so gated, but public hours vary and are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Neoclassical theatre facade on Boulevard Montmartre viewed from the pavement, a few minutes; interior entered only for performances so no normal visit inside.
judgement_basis: A theatre facade directly on the wide, traffic-heavy Boulevard Montmartre with no free seating and a quiet interior, but the boulevard is brightly lit and busy at all hours.
queue_basis: A performance theatre with no walk-in queue; entry is by show ticket and on a tour it is only viewed from the boulevard.

name: Place de la Bourse
short_description: Square dominated by the Palais Brongniart (former Paris Stock Exchange), built by Napoleon on the site of a razed convent

beats.script_body: The Paris Stock Exchange stands on the site of the convent of Les Filles de Saint-Thomas, which was closed during the Revolution. In the nascent age of capitalism, Napoleon had the convent razed and replaced it with this shrine to commerce, designed to emulate a Greek temple. For nearly two centuries it served as the nerve centre of French finance — though women were barred from entering until 1967, when Article XI prohibiting their admittance was finally repealed.
physical_cues: Stock Exchange building in Greek temple style dominates the square
beats.source_passage: The Paris Stock Exchange stands in its centre, on the site of the convent of Les Filles de Saint-Thomas, which was closed down during the Revolution

opening_hours_basis: An open public square viewed from the pavement, not gated, so hours are null.
visit_basis: Open square dominated by the colonnaded Palais Brongniart which you walk around to take in from several angles, about 18 minutes; the exchange building is not normally open to visit.
judgement_basis: An open square ringed by roads and parked cars around the Palais Brongniart, with no protective enclosure to stop a running child reaching traffic and no notable free quiet seating, but it is a central lit place with people passing at night.
queue_basis: An open public square with no gate or ticket; the whole value stands in the open with no line.

name: Notre-Dame-des-Victoires
short_description: 17th-century basilica on Place des Petits-Pères, a pilgrimage shrine co-designed by the architect of Les Invalides, where Lully is buried

beats.script_body: The painting above the high altar of Notre-Dame-des-Victoires tells a story of royal gratitude. It shows the Holy Virgin seated on a cloud, with Louis XIII at her feet presenting a plan of the church — his thanks for divine help defeating his enemies. To the King's right, a man surrenders the keys of the defeated town of La Rochelle, visible in the background. To his left stands Richelieu, whose initiative it was to eliminate the Huguenots and who obtained their surrender at La Rochelle in 1628. The illustrious architect of the Invalides, Libéral Bruant, collaborated in the construction of this pilgrimage church.
physical_cues: painting above the high altar showing Louis XIII presenting church plan
beats.source_passage: The painting above the high altar shows the Holy Virgin seated on a cloud: at her feet is Louis XIII presenting her with a plan of the church

beats.script_body: Among the famous Parisians buried at Notre-Dame-des-Victoires was Louis XIV's court composer Lully, whose funeral monument can still be seen between two side chapels. But the church itself had a turbulent afterlife: it was looted and wrecked during the Revolution, then found an unlikely second use as the Paris stock exchange between 1796 and 1809, before the Bourse moved to its purpose-built temple on Place de la Bourse.
physical_cues: Lully's funeral monument between two side chapels
beats.source_passage: Among famous Parisians who were buried here was Louis XIV's musician Lully. The church was looted and wrecked during the Revolution, then found use as the Paris stock exchange between 1796 and 1809

opening_hours_basis: A basilica you enter through doors, so gated, but its precise hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Modest facade on a small square takes a few minutes; inside is a basilica famous for its walls covered in thousands of votive plaques plus Lully's tomb, roughly 18 minutes.
judgement_basis: A church interior expecting silence, on the small quiet Place des Petits-Pères which has little through-traffic or nightlife, and the church itself is locked after hours, so I judge after-dark false on this calm side-street.
queue_basis: A basilica with an open door and no ticket or security check, entered directly without stopping.

name: Bibliotheque Nationale de France - Richelieu
short_description: Historic home of the French national library since 1721, housing 12 million books in Labrouste's celebrated reading room

beats.script_body: The Bibliothèque Nationale traces its origins to Charles V in the 14th century, when the king concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in a tower of the Louvre. The collection was scattered during the Hundred Years' War but gathered again in the 16th century by Louis XII and especially by the humanistic François I. Over the centuries it grew relentlessly — swollen first by the Revolution, when a prodigious flow of books confiscated from the aristocracy and religious institutions poured in, and then by the 19th-century explosion of printing. By the late 20th century the institution held over 12 million books, 6 million engravings, 800,000 coins and medals, and 400,000 records.
beats.source_passage: This monumental institution was initiated by Charles V in the 14th century, when he concentrated his ancestors' manuscripts in the tower of the Louvre

beats.script_body: In 1643, Cardinal Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs — the Hôtel Tubeuf — to keep close to Richelieu's Palais-Royal. Within two years he had acquired all the land extending north to the present rue Colbert, including a second mansion. He commissioned François Mansart to build a gallery between the two mansions to house his art collection, and then a separate wing for his library of 40,000 volumes — the most impressive in Europe. Mazarin had sent emissaries to every court and kingdom with orders to buy every book unavailable in Paris, acquiring between 30,000 and 35,000 volumes in less than ten years.
beats.source_passage: In 1643 Mazarin rented a property at 8 rue des Petits-Champs, the Hétel Tubeuf

opening_hours_basis: A library entered through doors/security, so gated, but its exact hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Long historic facade and entrance courtyard take ten minutes outside; inside are the restored Labrouste and Oval reading rooms plus a museum of treasures, roughly an hour with entry.
judgement_basis: A national library whose reading rooms demand absolute silence and offer no casual free seating to the public, but it stands on lit central streets near the Palais-Royal with people about in the evening.
queue_basis: Public access to the museum and gallery passes a reception and bag check that moves steadily, giving only a brief line at midday peak.

name: Galerie Vivienne
short_description: Elegant 1823 covered arcade with mosaic floors and neoclassical decor, one of the most beautiful passages in Paris

beats.script_body: Two hidden arcades lie side by side here — the highlight of the 2nd arrondissement. The Galerie Vivienne, with its tasteful, arty boutiques and good bookshops, has a charming, antiquated feel. Next door, the Galerie Colbert has been renovated into a more formal, classical compound in true French style, enhanced by its pale pink stone. Both offer an ideal refuge on a wet day — a glimpse of the covered-passage culture that once defined Parisian shopping.
physical_cues: Galerie Vivienne with arty boutiques and bookshops
Galerie Colbert with pale pink stone
beats.source_passage: On your left are two delightful hidden arcades - the highlight of the 2nd arrondissement - Galeries Vivienne and Colbert

opening_hours_basis: Gated covered arcade with grilles; OSM tag "Mo-Sa 08:30-20:30" transcribed with Sunday closed.
visit_basis: Elegant covered arcade with mosaic floors, glass roof and neoclassical shopfronts to walk slowly and browse, about 15 minutes; the arcade itself is the space.
judgement_basis: A narrow covered arcade with glass shopfronts at child height, only paid café tables, echoing acoustics, and gates locked after closing.
queue_basis: A covered arcade open at both ends with no door or ticket; visitors stroll through with no queue.

name: Square Louvois
short_description: Small garden on the site of a former opera house, with Visconti's fountain depicting four rivers of France

beats.script_body: Square Louvois stands on the site of Paris's ninth opera house. On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry — younger son of the future Charles X — was stabbed at the royal doorway of the theatre by a Bonapartist saddler named Louvel, as part of a scheme to rid France of the House of Bourbon. The Duke died the following day. Louvel was caught and guillotined before he could do more harm, and the King ordered the opera house razed to obliterate the scene of the crime. Today a graceful fountain by Visconti stands in its place, its allegorical figures representing the four biggest rivers of France that bear feminine names — which explains why the Rhône is not among them.
physical_cues: Visconti fountain with allegorical river figures
beats.source_passage: On 13 February 1820, the Duc de Berry, eldest son of the future Charles X, was assassinated at the royal doorway of the theatre

beats.script_body: Lully actually lived nearby, in the corner house at nos. 45 rue des Petits-Champs and 47 rue Sainte-Anne. Its listed façade is decorated with musical instruments and masks of Bacchantes and satyrs — a fitting home for the composer who dominated French music under Louis XIV. The street names around Square Louvois — Cherubini, Rameau and Lully — are the only reminders of the neighbourhood's lyrical past.
physical_cues: listed façade with musical instruments and masks at 45 rue des Petits-Champs / 47 rue Sainte-Anne
beats.source_passage: Lully actually lived near by, in the corner house at n°s 45 rue des Petits-Champs and 47 rue Sainte-Anne

beats.script_body: At no. 6 rue Rameau, at the beginning of the 19th century, lived the idolized tenor Adolphe Nourrit, who premiered all the masterpieces of his time — the works of Rossini and Meyerbeer among them. During a performance of Halévy's La Juive in Marseille, he suffered a vocal crisis that ended his career. Devastated, he threw himself from a window in Naples in 1839. He was only 37.
beats.source_passage: the idolized tenor Adolphe Nourrit, who premiered all the masterpieces of the time, lived at n° 6 rue Rameau

beats.script_body: Nearby rue Chabanais, opened in 1776, was famous above all for the internationally renowned brothel at no. 12, which from 1878 to 1946 catered to the exclusive clientele of the Jockey Club on Boulevard des Italiens. Most of the crowned heads of Europe frequented this impeccably tasteful establishment, as did ministers and government leaders of the Third Republic. Their visits were discreetly described on official timetables as 'visit to the President of the Sénat.' The splendid furniture was dispersed at auction at Drouot on 8 May 1951.
physical_cues: 18th-century mansions with wrought-iron decorations on rue Chabanais
beats.source_passage: rue Chabanais was famous first and foremost for its internationally renowned brothel at n° 12, which from 1878 to 1946 catered to the exclusive clientele

opening_hours_basis: A fenced public garden with closing gates, so gated, but its exact hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Small garden with benches and Visconti's four-rivers fountain to walk round and view, about 8 minutes; nothing to enter.
judgement_basis: A small fenced public garden set back from traffic with benches around Visconti's fountain, quiet enough to talk and enclosed enough for a child to run, but gated and locked at night like all Paris squares.
queue_basis: A small free public garden entered through an open gate with no ticket or check, so no line exists.

name: Passage Choiseul
short_description: Covered arcade built in 1825, once home to Parnasse poets, Anatole France, and Offenbach's winter Bouffes Parisiens theatre

beats.script_body: Passage de Choiseul, built in 1825, was once imbued with a rich cultural life. At no. 23 stood a publishing house that brought the Parnasse poets to the world — Sully Prudhomme, Leconte de Lisle, Heredia and François Coppée — followed from 1864 by Paul Verlaine. A few years later Anatole France worked here as editor for roughly a decade. At no. 73, the stage door to the winter Bouffes Parisiens still stands, where Jacques Offenbach, then director of the theatre, could be seen walking through during the winter seasons of 1855 to 1863.
physical_cues: stage door to winter Bouffes Parisiens at no. 73
beats.source_passage: Until 1965 n° 23 was the site of a publishing house which published the works of the Parnasse poets

opening_hours_basis: A covered arcade with grilles that close, so gated, but its exact hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Long covered arcade you walk through with shops and its literary history, about 10 minutes; the passage itself is the space.
judgement_basis: A long narrow covered arcade lined with shopfronts at child height, no free public seating, echoing under its glass roof, and closed off with gates after hours.
queue_basis: A covered public passage open at both ends with no door or ticket; you walk straight through.

name: Restaurant Drouant
short_description: Historic restaurant on Place Gaillon where the Goncourt literary prize has been awarded since 1914

beats.script_body: In the celebrated Drouant restaurant on the corner of 18 rue Gaillon, the Goncourt Prize — the most prestigious of French literary prizes — is awarded every third Monday of November. Charles Drouant came up to Paris from Alsace in 1880, one of many compatriots torn by the loss of their region to the Germans. His restaurant soon attracted artists and writers with its fresh oysters from Brittany, and Alphonse and Léon Daudet, Rodin, Renoir, and Edmond de Goncourt became regulars. On 10 December 1919, Léon Daudet brought Proust the letter announcing he had won the prize for À l'ombre des Jeunes Filles en fleurs — though by a narrow margin of six votes to four over Dorgelès's war novel Les Croix de Bois.
physical_cues: Drouant restaurant on corner of rue Gaillon
beats.source_passage: In the celebrated Drouant restaurant on the comer of 18 rue Gaillon, the Goncourt Prize, the most prestigious of French literary prizes, is awarded every third Monday of November

opening_hours_basis: A restaurant entered through a door, so gated, but its exact service hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Restaurant facade on the small Place Gaillon viewed from outside for its Goncourt-prize history, a few minutes; entering is a full meal, not a tour stop.
judgement_basis: A restaurant on the small Place Gaillon offering only paid seating and no run-around space, but the place is lit and lies just off the busy Avenue de l'Opéra quarter with people about at night.
queue_basis: A restaurant with no public queue for entry; on a walking tour it is a facade passed by, with dining by reservation not a standing line.

name: Harry's New York Bar
short_description: Legendary American bar opened in 1911, birthplace of the Bloody Mary cocktail, frequented by Hemingway and Fitzgerald

beats.script_body: At no. 5 rue Daunou, the red neon sign of Harry's Bar still beckons from a quiet, deserted street. This was a favourite haunt of Hemingway, whose photograph hangs on the wall, and of his friend Fitzgerald, who would drop in from the Ritz just round the corner. Opened in 1911, Harry's New York Bar was the heart of American expatriate Paris in the 1920s — and the birthplace of the Bloody Mary cocktail, mixed here by bartender Fernand Petiot in 1921.
physical_cues: red neon sign of Harry's Bar
beats.source_passage: At n° 5 the red neon sign of Harry's Bar still stands out in the night in the otherwise dark, deserted street

opening_hours_basis: A bar entered through a door, so gated, but its exact hours are not confidently known; left unfiltered.
visit_basis: Wood-panelled street frontage takes a few minutes outside; inside is a historic bar where you can sit for a Bloody Mary and take in the pennants and cellar piano, around 25 minutes.
judgement_basis: A bar interior with only paid seating and no space for children, on the lit and central rue Daunou near the Opéra where people are about in the evening.
queue_basis: A bar you walk into off the street with no ticket or security screening; any wait is for a seat inside, not a line to enter.

name: Rue de la Paix
short_description: Paris's most glamorous shopping street since the 19th century, birthplace of haute couture with Worth, Cartier and Paquin

beats.script_body: Rue de la Paix was once the site of the beautiful convent of the Capucines, closed during the Revolution and converted into a theatre. A popular funfair was held in its gardens and the famous Franconi moved his circus there. In 1806, Napoleon razed everything to make room for a glorious thoroughfare to honour his name, entrusting the project to his architects Percier and Fontaine. After his defeat in 1814, however, the street was renamed rue de la Paix to commemorate the Peace of Amiens.
beats.source_passage: once the site of the church of the beautiful convent of the Capucines. The convent was closed down during the Revolution

beats.script_body: At no. 7 was the house of Charles Frederick Worth, rightly claimed to be the first haute couture designer, who raised dressmaking from craft to art. When Worth arrived from England in 1845, aged 20, he had just 117 francs in his pocket and knew not a word of French. He had served seven years apprenticed to the drapers Swan and Edgar, and after 12 years of hard work in Paris opened his own house on rue de la Paix in 1858. His timing was perfect: this was the heyday of the glamorous Second Empire, where multitudes of social upstarts, ready to squander unlimited sums, accepted Worth's tyranny because they could not claim to be his social betters. The reign of the haute couture designer thus began.
beats.source_passage: At n° 7 was the house of Charles Worth, rightly claimed to be the first haute couture designer

beats.script_body: The head office of Cartier is still at no. 13 rue de la Paix. The house was founded in 1847 by Louis-François Cartier, who until then had been working for another famous jeweller, Adolphe Picard. He first set up shop near the Palais-Royal, then moved to the fashionable Boulevard des Italiens, where his customers included the Empress Eugénie and Napoleon III's cousin, la Princesse Mathilde. In 1899 his grandson Louis moved to rue de la Paix, by then the centre of luxury of the capital. Cartier's international clientele included Edward VII of England, Alfonso XIII of Spain, and the Duchess of Windsor.
physical_cues: Cartier head office at no. 13 rue de la Paix
beats.source_passage: The head office of the jeweller Cartier is still at n° 13 rue de la Paix. The house was founded in 1847 by Louis Ferdinand Cartier

beats.script_body: In 1892, the prosperous banker Paquin set up his wife at no. 5 rue de la Paix. Madame Jeanne Paquin was the first major woman couturier and also the first woman in fashion to be awarded the Légion d'honneur, in 1913. A prominent public figure, she chaired the fashion section of the 1900 Universal Exhibition. At its peak, 2,700 employees worked for her establishment, which was located above Robert's chemist shop — opened in 1820 by Dr Roberts, chemist and surgeon to the British Embassy, and now the sole reminder of the street's former glories among the travel agencies.
physical_cues: Robert's chemist shop still standing on rue de la Paix
beats.source_passage: Madame Paquin was the first woman designer and also the first woman to be awarded the Légion d'honneur in 1913

opening_hours_basis: An open public shopping street whose value stands in the open, so it is not gated.
visit_basis: Elegant shopping street of jewellers and couture houses running from the Opera to Place Vendome; walked end to end looking at the storefronts and the Vendome column vista, about 15-20 min, with no single interior that is the point of a visit.
judgement_basis: A wide luxury shopping street with vehicle traffic and no free public seating, its jewellery-shop windows fronting narrow pavements make it unsafe for a running child and offer nowhere to sit, but it is broad, well-lit and central enough for someone to be left standing at night.
queue_basis: An open shopping street with no gate or ticket; the whole value stands in the open, so there is no line to enter.
